item.title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.37691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.
item.dc:creator: Zzyv Zzyzek

item.title: Generating pivot Gray codes for spanning arborescences of complete digraphs and split digraphs in constant amortized time
item.description: arXiv:2610.37783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first known efficient algorithm to generate pivot Gray codes for spanning arborescences of complete digraphs, listing all spanning arborescences such that consecutive arborescences differ by reassigning the outgoing edge of exactly one vertex. Our recursive algorithm generates each spanning arborescence in constant amortized time using $O(n^2)$ space. We then extend our algorithm to generate the first known pivot Gray codes for spanning arborescences of split digraphs, achieving constant amortized time per arborescence using $ O(n^2) $ space. Finally, we further generalize our approach to proper interval digraphs. When the arborescences are rooted at the leftmost interval, our algorithm generates the pivot Gray code in constant amortized time per arborescence using $ {O}(n^2) $ space.
item.dc:creator: Bowie Liu, Dennis Wong

item.title: A Simple Optimistic B-Skiplist Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2610.37977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first optimistic concurrent B-skiplist, built on optimistic lock coupling (OLC). OLC replaces the multi-cache-line RW lock with a compact, single-cache-line lock: readers validate a version number without writing to shared memory, avoiding cache invalidations and retrying only on a detected conflict. Although OLC was thought poorly suited to skiplists, where a single per-element lock may span structurally unrelated levels, the B-skiplist's blocked layout places each level (and associated lock) in its own node. We exploit the B-skiplist's upfront knowledge of promotion height with a hybrid top-down scheme that traverses upper levels optimistically and locks only from the promotion level down, so most inserts never dirty a cache line. On 128 threads, the proposed optimistic B-skiplist achieves $1.2-10\times$ higher throughput over state-of-the-art concurrent skiplist implementations. Furthermore, the optimistic B-skiplist achieves $0.8-4.3\times$ the throughput compared to high-performance optimistic B+-tree implementations based on RW locks and OLC. Finally, the optimistic B-skiplist achieves up to $13\times$ lower latency than concurrent skiplists and tree-based indices, and is within $1.6\times$ of the latency of the OLC-based B+-tree.
item.dc:creator: Jianting Guo, Yicong Luo, Helen Xu

item.title: Output-Sensitive Enumeration of Maximal Closed Substrings in Linear Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.38114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the output-sensitive enumeration of maximal closed substrings (MCSs). Given a string of length $n$ over an integer alphabet, let $k$ denote its number of MCS occurrences. We combine a right-to-left sweep on the string with range-successor queries to obtain all MCSs with two deterministic word-RAM bounds: for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we can report all MCSs in $O(n\sqrt{\log n}+k\log^\varepsilon n)$ time using $O(n)$ words of space, or in $O(n\sqrt{\log n}+k\log\log n)$ time using $O(n\log\log n)$ words. Both bounds include preprocessing and report occurrences by their endpoints. In particular, these algorithms improve the known $O(n\log n)$ worst-case time bound for sufficiently small output.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Fischer, Dominik K\"oppl

item.title: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.38133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search algorithms like HNSW, DiskANN, NSG, and others have surged in popularity in recent years due to their excellent empirical performance in comparison to space-partitioning methods like IVF data structures and Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH). However, in contrast to LSH and related methods, obtaining strong worst-case theoretical guarantees for graph-based search has proven challenging. In this paper, we prove a strong lower bound that helps explain the lack of progress towards such guarantees. We show that no standard graph-based method (any that runs a variant of greedy search on a flat or hierarchical graph) can achieve sublinear query time for approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space, even for an arbitrarily large approximation factor. On the other hand, we prove that sublinear query time is possible if we allow for Steiner points in the search graph. We obtain bounds comparable to LSH, showing e.g., that graph-based search with Steiner points can solve $c$-approximate nearest neighbor search in Euclidean space with query time $\tilde{O}(n^{1/(c-1)})$. We complement this result with initial experiments exploring how Steiner points can be incorporated into practical graph-based methods.
item.dc:creator: Majid Daliri, Mohammadreza Daneshvaramoli, Purna Dutta, Edo Liberty, Cameron Musco, Christopher Musco, Torsten Suel

item.title: Fast Sparse $\alpha$-Navigable Graph Construction with Improved Resource Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2610.38205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based nearest neighbor search methods, which run greedy search on a directed graph over the data points, have surged in popularity in recent years. A common goal is to construct a search graph with the $\alpha$-navigability property, which ensures that greedy search returns provably good approximate nearest neighbors and converges in few iterations. Increasing $\alpha \geq 1$ improves accuracy and convergence rate, but requires more edges, which increases both space and search time. This tradeoff has motivated the study of algorithms for constructing a sparsest $\alpha$-navigable graph for a given set of points. For any point set and any distance function, we show how to compute an $\alpha$-navigable graph with at most $O(\log n)$ times as many edges as the sparsest $(1+\varepsilon)\alpha$-navigable graph, in $O(n^\omega \log(\Delta)/\varepsilon)$ time, where $\omega < 2.372$ is the matrix multiplication exponent and $\Delta$ is the aspect ratio of the input. This improves on Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (SODA 2026), who achieve the same runtime but are only competitive with the sparsest $2(1+\varepsilon)\alpha$-navigable graph. Since sparsity often increases rapidly with $\alpha$ (typically $\alpha \leq 1.1$), their bound can be significantly weaker. Previously, the best algorithm competing with the sparsest $(1+\varepsilon)\alpha$-navigable graph required $\widetilde{O}(n^{2.5})$ time. Our techniques also extend to constructing sparse $\tau$-monotonic graphs, another popular target in nearest neighbor search. Finally, we give a fine-grained complexity analysis suggesting that improving the $O(n^\omega)$ running time is unlikely, or would require a very different approach. It is based on hardness results for problems related to verifying whether a graph is navigable, a topic of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Alex Conway, Laxman Dhulipala, Martin Farach-Colton, Ben Landrum, Christopher Musco, Yarin Shechter, Torsten Suel, Richard Wen

item.title: Optimal Encodings for Next/Previous Larger/Smaller Value Queries: A Unified Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.38327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a 1D array over a total order and a query position in the array, a next larger value query returns the nearest position to the right whose value is larger than the value at the query position. Next smaller value queries and previous larger/smaller value queries are defined analogously. These queries are closely related to the $k$-th range minimum/maximum problem, which asks for the position of the $k$-th leftmost minimum/maximum value when the query range contains multiple minimum/maximum values. In this paper, we consider the encoding problem for answering any arbitrary subfamily of these four queries, where the queries must be answered without accessing the input array. We give a unified approach for obtaining space lower bounds for such encodings. We also obtain data structures for the query subfamilies that match the lower bounds up to lower-order additive terms, while supporting the queries in constant time. Our results generalize and improve several previous results on this problem [Gawrychowski and Nicholson, ICALP-2015; Jo and Satti, TCS-2016; Tsur, IPL-2019; Jo and Kim, Algorithmica-2025]. In addition, these results give tight bounds on the encoding complexity of all subfamilies of these queries for (1) permutations, (2) arrays without consecutive equal elements, and (3) general arrays.
item.dc:creator: Seungbum Jo, Geunho Kim, Kunihiko Sadakane, Srinivasa Rao Satti

item.title: Estimating the number of nodes and paths in a DAG by following a random path
item.description: arXiv:2610.38586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a simple method to compute an unbiased estimate of the number of nodes of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) by following a random directed path. This method is due to Leonard Pitt from 1987, and it generalizes a method of D. E. Knuth from the 1960s for estimating the size of a rooted tree. A slight variation makes it possible to estimate the number of source-sink paths. We extend the algorithm to use many "agents" that walk cooperatively through the graph. This extension unifies and generalizes several methods that have been proposed for approximately counting the nodes of a tree.
item.dc:creator: G\"unter Rote

item.title: Fully Dynamic All-Pairs Min Cuts on Planar Graphs via Planar Pattern Emulators
item.description: arXiv:2610.38730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fully-dynamic all-pairs minimum cut problem on planar graphs. Given an $n$-vertex undirected planar graph $G=(V,E)$ undergoing edge insertions and deletions, the goal is to efficiently process these updates while supporting $s$-$t$ minimum cut queries for any pair of vertices $s$ and $t$. We give a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate dynamic algorithm that supports edge updates and minimum cut queries in $n^{o(1)}$ time, for any $1/\text{poly}(\log n) < \varepsilon < 1$. For general graphs, previous results either are limited to partially dynamic settings or achieve only logarithmic-factor approximations. The main conceptual and technical contribution is to show that a suitable adaptation of the planar emulator of Chang, Krauthgamer, and Tan~[STOC'22] satisfies the stronger pattern emulator introduced by Chen and Tan~[ICALP'25]. This leads almost immediately to a nearly linear-time construction of pattern emulators, which, when combined with the recent fully dynamic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate all-pairs shortest paths algorithm of Filtser, Goranci, Patel, and Probst Gutenberg~[FOCS'24], yields our result.
item.dc:creator: Arnold Filtser, Gramoz Goranci, Ali Momeni, Neel Patel, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg

item.title: Dynamic $(\Delta+1)$ Vertex Coloring with Adaptive Adversaries: Entropy Compression to the Rescue
item.description: arXiv:2610.38787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a randomized algorithm for maintaining a $(\Delta+1)$ vertex coloring of a fully dynamic graph against an adaptive adversary with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ amortized update time. Our algorithm improves upon the recent randomized algorithms of Behnezhad, Rajaraman, and Wasim (SODA 2025) with $\tilde{O}(n^{8/9})$ and Flin and Halld\'orsson (ICALP 2025) with $\tilde{O}(n^{2/3})$ amortized update time. Our result (nearly) matches a fundamental limit of $O(\sqrt{n})$ update time identified by Flin and Halld\'orsson and settles their main open question. The previous algorithms' main improvement came from efficient coloring of the dense parts of the graph. Our approach complements these prior work by handling the sparse parts more efficiently, using ideas inspired by the recently developed dynamic entropy compression method. A key new aspect of our work is to tailor this method specifically to dynamic algorithms---as opposed to original local search algorithms---and achieve update times that can be sublinear in the number of involved constraints per update.
item.dc:creator: Sepehr Assadi, Helia Yazdanyar

item.title: Fast Perfect $L_2$ Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.38860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Perfect $L_2$ sampling is a powerful primitive for turnstile data streams, allowing algorithms to extract an index with probability proportional to its squared frequency, with applications to dynamic join size estimation, query optimization, heavy-hitters, sampling from self-joins, and real-time monitoring of evolving datasets. The setting $p=2$ is also the largest $p$ for which $L_p$ sampling can be achieved in polylogarithmic space. However, existing space-optimal perfect samplers rely on explicit polynomial duplication, requiring inefficient polynomial update times per stream arrival. Resolving a open question left by Swartworth, Woodruff, and Zhou [FOCS 2025], we present a perfect $L_2$ sampler that achieves an expected $\text{polylog}(n)$ update time while maintaining an optimal $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log^3 n)$ bits of space.
item.dc:creator: David P. Woodruff, Samson Zhou

item.title: Fully Dynamic Unconstrained Submodular Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.38865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study unconstrained maximization of a fixed nonnegative submodular function when the ground set changes by insertions and deletions. A uniformly random subset gives a $1/4$-approximation with constantly many value-oracle queries per update. We obtain improvements over this bound for arbitrary oblivious update sequences, without knowing future deletions. For value estimation, we give a $(\sqrt2-1-\varepsilon)$-approximation using $O_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\log^2(N+1))$ expected amortized oracle queries, with failure probability at most $\delta$ at each fixed time. Here $N$ bounds the number of active elements. The algorithm maintains Poisson samples of the positive mass of random chain lower bounds. We prove that the factor $\sqrt2-1$ is tight for this certificate, even when polynomially many independent orders are used. For every fixed integer $K\ge2$, we maintain a feasible $(1/4+\Omega(K^{-2}))$-approximate set using $\widetilde O_K(N^{1/K})$ amortized queries. Thus every fixed exponent $\gamma>0$ permits a fixed improvement over $1/4$ with $\widetilde O_\gamma(N^\gamma)$ update queries. In the square-root regime, a stronger algorithm attains $\rho_{\rm sq}-\varepsilon$, where $\rho_{\rm sq}>0.3177$. The maintained sets are feasible after every update, and their approximation guarantees hold in expectation. All bounds count oracle queries; the value estimator may query previously seen inactive elements, whereas the set algorithms use only currently active elements.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Hajiaghayi

item.title: Dimension Reduction and Coresets for Min-Sum $k$-Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2610.38920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The min-sum $k$-clustering problem asks to partition an input of $n$ points into $k$ clusters so as to minimize the total pairwise distance within clusters. It is a natural alternative to center-based objectives when the data is not well captured by a small set of representative points. We study for this problem two standard sketching methods, dimension reduction and coresets, which represent the input more compactly while preserving the min-sum cost of every $k$-partition up to $1\pm\varepsilon$ factor. Our first contribution addresses dimension reduction in Euclidean space. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) Lemma readily implies that a random linear map to target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ preserves, with high probability, the min-sum cost of all $k$-partitions. We show that target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}(ddim\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log k+\log\log n))$ suffices for Euclidean inputs of doubling dimension at most $ddim$, and moreover this bound is nearly optimal. We also show that target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log k+\log\Delta))$ suffices for Euclidean inputs of aspect ratio at most $\Delta$. Our second contribution is to design the first $\varepsilon$-coreset for metric min-sum $k$-clustering. It is actually a movement-based coreset, has size $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(ddim)} k\log n$ for inputs of doubling dimension at most $ddim$, and can be constructed in randomized near-linear-time. We further use these coresets to design streaming algorithms for the problem.
item.dc:creator: Asaf Dallal, Robert Krauthgamer

item.title: Local Important Separators with Applications to Unbreakable Decomposition and Multicut
item.description:
arXiv:2610.39030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first local FPT algorithm for finding important separators: Given an undirected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, vertices $s,t$ and parameters $k$ and $
u$, we can enumerate all $s$-$t$ important separators of size at most $k$ and volume at most $
u$ in time $	ilde{O}(
u 2^{O(k)})$. Known approaches spend either $\Omega(m)$ time (not local) or $
u^{\Omega(k)}$ time (not FPT). Using this local algorithm, we show the following applications. (1) The first is an improved construction of unbreakable decomposition, a powerful generalization of tree decompositions. For any $k$, we can compute a $(5k,k)$-unbreakable decomposition with adhesion $4k$ in $	ilde{O}(k^{O(k)}m)$ time. This strictly subsumes the result of Anand, Lee, Li, Long, and Saranurak (SODA 2025) and is faster than the recent $O(k^{O(k^2)}m)$-time algorithm by Korhonen (STOC 2025) when $k = \omega\Bigl(\sqrt{ rac{\log \log n}{\log \log \log n}}\Bigr)$. Our algorithm is also simpler than that of Korhonen (STOC 2025). (2) We give a near-linear time algorithm for single-sink important separators. For any sink $t$, we can list all $v$-$t$ important separators of size at most $k$ across all $v \in V(G)$ in time $	ilde{O}(2^{O(k)}m)$. Known approaches trivially compute $v$-$t$ important separators for each $v$, taking $\Omega(4^k k mn)$ time. (3) Using the above result on single-sink important separators, we speed up undirected shadow removal and give the first almost-linear time FPT algorithm for Edge Multicut.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Anand, Euiwoong Lee, Yaowei Long, Thatchaphol Saranurak

item.title: Building On Learning-Augmented Online Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.39105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online sorting is a problem that has gained attention recently, and is a natural translation of sorting into an online setting. The problem at hand is to place elements of an online sequence immediately and irrevocably with the goal of producing an array that is as close to sorted as possible upon inserting all elements. Recent work by Bercea et al. [ESA 2026] introduced the incorporation of learned predictions into the online sorting domain. They show lower bounds for the consistency and robustness of any algorithm, including randomization, then provide a deterministic algorithm that is $O(n/r)$-consistent and $O(r)$-robust, which are tight bounds. However, this algorithm requires prior knowledge of the optimal offline cost of the full input sequence before all elements have been revealed. We resolve this by providing an algorithm with matching bounds that does not require knowledge of the optimal cost, then extend these results to the more general problem of online metric TSP, in line with the prior work.
item.dc:creator: Wyatt Olson

item.title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Size of Order Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.39311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Order graphs were introduced by Arroyuelo et al.\ (TODS 2024) as a generalization of the ring index, to support worst-case optimal joins on relations of arity $d$ while storing as few columns as possible: the index stores one column per edge, so its size is proportional to the number of edges of an order graph. It was known that the minimum number of edges lies between $\Omega(2^d\sqrt d)$ and $O(2^d d)$, and the lower bound had been claimed to be $42$ for $d=6$. We first exhibit an order graph with only $40$ edges for $d=6$, and show that the proof of that lower bound holds only for unions of cycles, whereas order graphs can be smaller than the smallest set of cycles. We give a corrected statement and proof that holds for every order graph: there must be at least $\max_m\binom dm\lceil m/2\rceil$ edges. This bound is $40$ for $d=6$, so our $40$-edge graph is optimal. We then settle the asymptotic question: the minimum size is $\Theta(2^d\sqrt d)$. This is obtained via an explicit construction, based on symmetric chain decompositions of the Boolean lattice, with at most $(d-1)\binom{d}{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}+2^d$ edges. The upper bound is within a factor $4+O(d^{-1/2})$ of the lower bound, and both numerically and asymptotically better than trie switching.
item.dc:creator: Ruben Becker, Adri\'an G\'omez-Brand\'on, Gonzalo Navarro, Nicola Prezza

item.title: Substring Complexity in BWT-Runs Bounded Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.39482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a string $T[1..n]$, its substring complexity is defined as $\delta=\max_k d_k/k$, where $d_k$ is the number of its distinct substrings of length $k$ in $T$. We show how to compute it in $O(n+r\log r)$ time, using only $O(r)$ words of space, where $r$ denotes the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Fischer

item.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Non-Splitting Coflow Scheduling in Heterogeneous Parallel Networks via Iterative Relaxation
item.description: arXiv:2610.39564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coflows capture the collective communication requirements of data-parallel applications, and scheduling them well is essential to the performance of modern data centers. We study non-splitting coflow scheduling in a heterogeneous parallel network whose $m$ network cores may be Electronic Packet Switches (EPS), not-all-stop Optical Circuit Switches (OCS), or all-stop OCS, where every flow must be transmitted entirely through a single core. Previous approximation algorithms for this setting have guarantees that grow linearly with the number of cores $m$ or with the maximum flow degree $\tau$ of a port, and therefore become weak as data centers deploy more cores. The source of this dependence is the rounding step: rounding each flow to the core holding its largest fractional value can inflate the load of a port by a factor of $m$. We replace this step with an iterative relaxation rounding scheme that handles the input-port and output-port capacity constraints simultaneously. For minimizing the makespan, this yields approximation ratios of $\min\{\tau, 3\}$, $2\min\{\tau, 3\}$, and $4\min\{\tau, 3\}$ for pure EPS, pure not-all-stop OCS, and pure all-stop OCS networks, respectively. For minimizing the total weighted coflow completion time, we obtain approximation ratios of $8\min\{\tau, 4\}$, $16\min\{\tau, 4\}$, and $32\min\{\tau, 4\}$ for the same three architectures. In a hybrid network, the guarantee is governed by the weakest architecture present, so the overall ratios are at most $4\min\{\tau,3\}\le 12$ and $32\min\{\tau,4\}\le 128$, respectively. Unlike all previous guarantees for non-splitting coflow scheduling in heterogeneous parallel networks, these bounds are absolute constants that do not grow with the number of cores $m$ or with the flow degree $\tau$. We also show that the integrality gap of the underlying linear program is at least $2$.
item.dc:creator: Chi-Yeh Chen

item.title: Parameterized Approximation of Max k-Weight CSP: A Dichotomy for Boolean Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.39751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study \textsc{Max $k$-Weight CSP}: maximize the satisfied weight of Boolean constraints with nonnegative rational weights by setting at most $k$ variables to $1$. Each constraint uses at most $d$ distinct variables and a relation from a finite Boolean language $\Gamma$. This includes \textsc{Partial Vertex Cover}, \textsc{Densest $k$-Subgraph}, bounded-frequency \textsc{Maximum Coverage}, and cardinality-constrained \textsc{Max-SAT}. We completely classify the fixed finite languages admitting an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (EPAS) with parameter $k+d$. Only nonempty relations excluding the all-zero tuple matter. For such a relation, a coordinate is a \emph{unit witness} if the tuple with a single $1$ in that coordinate is accepted, and a \emph{control} otherwise. A relation is \emph{Direct} if setting any selected control to $0$, with all other coordinates unchanged, preserves satisfaction. It is \emph{Rooted} if every satisfying tuple has a selected unit witness such that keeping it, setting all other unit witnesses to $0$, and setting any subset of selected controls to $0$ preserves satisfaction. If all such relations are Direct, or all are Rooted, we give a deterministic $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for every rational $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ in time $2^{O(d+k\log(1+dk/\varepsilon))}\ell_{\mathrm{in}}^{O(1)}$, where $\ell_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the total input length. The algorithms are uniform in $d$ and give an EPAS parameterized by $k+d$ whenever relation membership is polynomial-time decidable. If neither condition holds, no EPAS exists unless $\mathsf{FPT}=\mathsf{W[1]}$, even for unweighted instances where no two constraints involve the same set of variables.
item.dc:creator: Rudranarayan Kar, Souvik Saha, Abhishek Sahu

item.title: Four-Coloring Planar Graphs in Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.39753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The famous Four Color Theorem (4CT) states that any planar graph can be colored with four colors, but how do we find a 4-coloring? In our previous paper [FOCS'26], we presented a simple combinatorial algorithm to 4-color planar graphs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We improve it here to $O(n)$ time, which is optimal. The algorithm from our previous paper is based on proving that every planar triangulation has a linear number of reducible configurations or obstructing cycles. The bottleneck for the algorithm is that we need $O(\log n)$ Kempe changes to extend a recursive 4-coloring to the reducible configurations. Each Kempe change can involve a constant fraction of the graph and takes linear time. Here we show that all $O(\log n)$ Kempe changes can be identified and implemented in $O(n)$ time. The idea is to spend $O(n)$ time to preprocess the graph so that we can identify and simulate each good Kempe change in $O(n/\log n)$ amortized time. Thus, we implement all $O(\log n)$ Kempe changes in $O(n)$ total time. Based on this, we implement the whole 4-coloring in linear time. We note that creating such a representation for fast identification and simulation of the right Kempe changes is a challenge of data structures, unlike the previous paper that builds on a new graph theoretic understanding of reducible configurations.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, Carsten Thomassen, Mikkel Thorup

item.title: A Single-Exponential Time Algorithm for the Maximum-Cardinality Weakly Stable Matching Problem with Ties and Incomplete Lists
item.description: arXiv:2610.39764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Stable Marriage with Ties and Incomplete lists (SMTI) under weak stability. For an instance with $n$ agents on each side, we give an exact algorithm that returns a maximum-cardinality weakly stable matching in $O^*(22.74^n)$ time. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exact algorithm for this problem running in single-exponential time.
item.dc:creator: Shuichi Miyazaki, Suguru Tamaki

item.title: From Trees to Binary Trees: Approximation Algorithms and a PTAS
item.description: arXiv:2610.39863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kellerhals, Krebs, Nichterlein, and Schmid introduced the optimization problem Tree in Binary Tree (TBT), where, given a tree $T$, the task is to find a binary tree $S^*$ with $V(T)=V(S^*)$ that minimizes $\sum_{uv\in E(T)} \operatorname{dist}_{S^*}(u,v)$. They also introduced the variant Tree in Binary Tree With Steiner Nodes (TBT-SN), where the condition $V(T)=V(S^*)$ is relaxed to $V(T)\subseteq V(S^*)$. We give a simple linear-time $\frac{8}{3}$-approximation algorithm for TBT and a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for TBT-SN. Our main building idea in both algorithms is to iteratively consider subtrees of the tree $T$ which contain all vertices below some vertex $v$ and construct a solution where $v$ has degree 1. For the PTAS, we cut $T$ into smaller trees, solve these instances, modify the obtained solutions, and combine them to achieve a solution for the original instance.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Weisbrodt, Florian Werner

item.title: Communication-Oblivious Permutation and Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.39922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the help of secure hardware such as trusted execution environments (TEEs), private data can be uploaded and computed in untrusted cloud clusters, so that an adversary controlling the cloud can only see the data in encrypted form. However, the communication pattern between the processors may still reveal sensitive information about the data, so it is important to develop parallel algorithms in the BSP model whose communication pattern is independent of the input data, a property known as \textit{communication obliviousness}. In this paper, we study such algorithms for three fundamental problems: permutation, sorting, and 0-1 sorting. For the first two problems, we prove a tight (up to lower-order terms) communication complexity of $(2-2/p)n\pm o(n)$. Here, $p$ is the number of processors and $n$ is the input size, assuming $2\le p$ and $p=o(n^{1/3})$. Our lower bound holds regardless of the number of rounds and local memory size, while for balanced permutation and sorting the upper bound is achieved in a constant number of rounds with load at most $n/p+o(n/p)$. For 0-1 sorting, we also derive a tight communication complexity of $C_{\mathrm{cut}}(p) \cdot n \pm o(n)$, where $C_{\mathrm{cut}}(p)$ is the optimal value of a linear program parameterized by $p$. Although there appears to be no closed-form for $C_{\mathrm{cut}}(p)$, we show that it is strictly smaller than $2-2/p$ for all $p\ge 3$, thus separating 0-1 sorting from general sorting in terms of their communication complexity.
item.dc:creator: Qi Dong, Yilei Wang, Ke Yi

item.title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
item.description: arXiv:2610.39992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-\gamma)n})$, for a fixed $\gamma>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Kutzkov

item.title: Nearly Optimal Sparse Navigable Graphs in General Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.40146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study approximation algorithms for constructing sparse navigable graphs in general metrics. Given an $n$-point metric $(P,d)$ and a parameter $\alpha\ge1$, a directed graph on $P$ is $\alpha$-navigable if, for every pair of distinct points $s,t\in P$, the source $s$ has an outgoing neighbor $p$ with $d(p,t)<d(s,t)/\alpha$. The objective is to minimize the number of edges. Recent independent works of Khanna, Padaki, and Waingarten (2026) and Conway et al. (2026) give $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithms and show that an $o(\log n)$ approximation is NP-hard in general. Before our work, the best known running time for such an approximation for general $\alpha\ge1$ was $\widetilde O(\min\{n\operatorname{OPT}_\alpha,n^{2.5}\})$, where $\operatorname{OPT}_\alpha$ is the minimum number of edges in an $\alpha$-navigable graph. In this paper, we give a randomized algorithm that, with high probability, runs in $\widetilde O(n^2)$ time and achieves an $O(\log n)$ approximation for every $\alpha\ge1$. In general, these guarantees are nearly optimal up to constant factors in the approximation and polylogarithmic factors in the running time.
item.dc:creator: Hongyi Chen, Tianyi Zhang

item.title: Retrieval Sequencing in a Compact Storage System with Side Access
item.description: arXiv:2610.40169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a compact storage system with side access, bins are arranged in adjacent vertical stacks. In each retrieval cycle, bins blocking access are lifted to create a temporary tunnel through which a robot extracts one requested bin from the side. The lifted bins are then lowered again, and the energy expenditure of the cycle equals the number of lifted bins. Given a pick list known in advance, we seek a retrieval order that minimizes total energy expenditure. For every number of stacks, we prove that the total energy separates into an instance constant and a pairwise penalty, and that every energy-optimal order is laminar within each stack. For two stacks, we prove that the retrieval sequencing problem is solvable in polynomial time. For three stacks, we give an exact polynomial-time reduction to a merge problem and characterize which merge-problem instances arise from the storage model. We define a recursive class of retrieval orders and construct a polynomial-time dynamic program that minimizes energy expenditure over this class. Finally, we quantify the additional energy savings from batching, which allows several requested bins to be retrieved in one cycle.
item.dc:creator: Ya\u{g}mur G\"ul

item.title: Layering and reverse extension for weighted $k$-path vertex cover
item.description: arXiv:2610.40281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the weighted $k$-path vertex cover problem for any fixed integer $k \ge 2$, in which a vertex non-negatively weighted simple graph $G = (V, E)$ is given and one wants to find a minimum-weight vertex subset $C \subseteq V$ such that every simple path on $k$ vertices in $G$ contains at least one vertex of $C$. The problem generalizes the classic weighted vertex cover problem, that is, $k = 2$, and it admits a $k$-approximation algorithm of Hochbaum~[SIAM J. Comput., 1982] and a $(k - \frac 12)$-approximation algorithm of Br\"ustle et al.~[IWOCA 2021]. In this paper, we carefully design local weight functions in the Layering and Reverse Extension local ratio framework of Bar-Yehuda et al.~[ACM Comput. Surv., 2004], leading to an approximation algorithm of ratio $\frac {3k-1}4$ for odd $k \ge 3$ and of ratio $\frac {3k}4$ for even $k \ge 4$. When $k = 3$ and $k = 4$, these ratios are $2$ and $3$, respectively, matching the state-of-the-art approximation ratios for the corresponding special cases.
item.dc:creator: Jiajing Wu, An Zhang, Shiming Li, Guohui Lin

item.title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
item.description: arXiv:2610.40290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.
item.dc:creator: Dimitris Fotakis, Laurent Gourv\`es, Aris Pagourtzis, Panagiotis Patsilinakos

item.title: Half-Optimal Induced Matchings in Random Graphs: Online and Low-Degree Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.40369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For many optimization problems on random graphs, most prominently the largest independent set problem, natural algorithms reach only half the optimum, and such factor-two gaps are known to be sharp within broad algorithmic classes. We prove such a gap for finding large induced matchings in Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs. In the worst case, requiring a matching to be induced turns a polynomial-time solvable problem into an NP-hard one; our results reveal an average-case counterpart. In $G(n,p)$ with $C/n\le p\le 1-\kappa$, the largest induced matching has size $(1+o(1))L$ with high probability, where $L=\log_{1/(1-p)}(np)$. A simple online greedy algorithm finds an induced matching of size $(1/2-\epsilon)L$, while no online algorithm, even with adaptive inspection order and unbounded computation, finds one of size $(1/2+\epsilon)L$ except with probability $\exp(-\Omega(L\log(np)))$. In the sparse regime $p=d/n$, low-degree polynomial algorithms exhibit the same sharp threshold. Our guarantees rest on a maximality principle: with high probability, every maximal induced matching is half-optimal. Greedy outputs a maximal induced matching and our low-degree algorithm a near-maximal one. We bypass the delicate coupling arguments classically used to analyze greedy since Karp. For low-degree hardness, we adapt Wein's overlap gap argument, with forbidden structures that track overlaps between endpoint sets rather than edge sets, since a new edge may join two previously used endpoints and thus encounter no fresh randomness. For online hardness, we give a new and significantly simpler argument that avoids the correlated instances of prior OGP-based proofs: at a suitable stopping time, all pairs involving uninspected vertices remain unrevealed, so a direct first-moment bound suffices.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Dhawan, Eren C. K{\i}z{\i}lda\u{g}, Neeladri Maitra, Cheng Mao, Timothy L. H. Wee

item.title: Zero-freeness for Random Regular Graphs up to the Replica Symmetry Breaking Threshold
item.description: arXiv:2610.40510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study antiferromagnetic spin systems on random regular graphs through the lens of the phase transitions characterized by the complex zeros of the partition function. Our motivating examples include the hardcore model and the antiferromagnetic Potts model (including proper $q$-colorings at $\beta=0$). For both models on random $d$-regular graphs, we establish, with high probability over the graph, zero-free regions throughout the interior of the replica-symmetric regime. Asymptotically, this regime extends up to tree occupation density $$\alpha < \alpha_{\mathrm{RSB}}(d) = (2\log d - 2\log\log d + 2 - 2\log 2 + o_d(1))/d$$ for the hardcore model and up to degree $$d < d_{\mathrm{RSB}}(q) = (2q-1)\log q - 2\log 2 + o_q(1)$$ for proper $q$-colorings. Leveraging the standard algorithmic implications of zero-freeness, we obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms that multiplicatively approximate the corresponding partition functions at fixed rational parameters throughout this regime, with high probability over the graph. Our algorithmic guarantees significantly improve upon prior work and extend beyond the parameter ranges reached by previously known search algorithms. To establish our results, we first develop reinforced small subgraph conditioning, which resolves short-cycle fluctuations in the complex plane by lifting classical small subgraph conditioning on random regular graphs to random holomorphic functions. Second, we overcome the standard second-moment barrier caused by the exponential blowup of the bare second moment inside the replica-symmetric phase, by showing that replica symmetry implies a nonpositive Bethe functional and upgrading planted overlap concentration to an exponentially small bound, which enables a typical-graph truncation that controls complex second moments up to the replica symmetry breaking threshold.
item.dc:creator: Zejia Chen, Chunyang Wang, Xinyuan Zhang

item.title: Exact Competitive Ratios of Index Rules for Scheduling with Obligatory Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.40554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit scheduling with obligatory testing, where each job consists of two operations: a test with an initially known time and an operation whose processing time is revealed upon completion of the job's test. We develop an iterative competitive-ratio-preserving instance-reduction method that enables us to compute exact competitive ratios directly on highly structured instances for various index rules. Our main result is a clean analysis showing that the competitive ratio of the algorithm $1$-SORT is exactly the Golden Ratio $\varphi\approx 1.618$, improving the recent best-known upper bound of $1.861$ for arbitrary testing times. We further leverage this method to obtain near-tight bounds for a simple randomized algorithm on instances with uniform testing times.
item.dc:creator: Felix Buld

item.title: The Tight Competitive Ratio of Greedy for Online Steiner Forest
item.description: arXiv:2610.40569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The online Steiner Forest problem is a fundamental network design problem in which terminal pairs arrive one at a time and an algorithm must irrevocably purchase edges connecting each pair. The natural greedy algorithm connects each terminal pair by a shortest path after making all previously purchased edges free. Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal (SODA 1996) proved that this algorithm is $O(log^2 k)$-competitive and conjectured an $O(log k)$ bound, where $k$ is the number of terminal pairs. Bamas, Drygala, and Maggiori (SODA 2022) obtained an $O(\log \NumPairs\log\log \NumPairs)$ bound for greedy on a restricted class of inputs, leaving the general case open. In this paper, we resolve the competitive ratio of the greedy algorithm for online Steiner Forest, proving that it is tightly $\Theta(log(k) log log(k))$. Specifically, we establish an $O(log(k) log log(k))$ upper bound for arbitrary instances and construct a matching $\Omega(log(k) log log(k))$ lower bound. Our results refute the $O(log k)$ conjecture of Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal and establish a tight $\Theta(log log k)$ separation between the greedy algorithm and the best possible online algorithm for Steiner Forest.
item.dc:creator: Iman Gholami, Ilya Hajiaghayi, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Peyman Jabbarzade

item.title: Minimum Label $k$-Cut on Planar Graphs: Complexity and Color Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.40575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimum Label $k$-Cut asks for a minimum-size set of colors such that deleting all edges of these colors leaves at least $k$ connected components. We study how the structure of the underlying graph and its color classes affects the complexity of this problem. Regarding fixed-parameter tractability with respect to $k$ on simple planar graphs, we prove that the problem is W[1]-hard, even when the underlying graph is a cactus graph and each color appears at most twice. Furthermore, for cactus graphs in which every color class is connected, we establish a complexity boundary in terms of the maximum monochromatic degree: when this degree is at most two, an optimal solution can be found in $O(Nk^2)$ time, where $N$ is the input size, with no restriction on color frequency or the number of blocks spanned by a color; allowing the maximum monochromatic degree to increase to three already makes the decision version NP-complete. Finally, we prove that the problem remains W[1]-hard parameterized by $k$ on fan graphs, even when every color class is an induced path. These results show that bounding color frequency does not suffice to eliminate parameterized hardness. They also establish a monochromatic-degree boundary for connected colors on cactus graphs and identify complexity barriers to extending this tractable case to outerplanar graphs.
item.dc:creator: Yuanhao Wang, Wei Wang

item.title: Maximum Cardinality Matching in $n^{2+o(1)}$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.40591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the maximum cardinality matching problem in general graphs, and give an $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm for the problem. Our work builds on recent work on combinatorial algorithms for maximum flow and extends the techniques to skew-symmetric flow problems which capture general matchings as a special case.
item.dc:creator: George Z. Li, Jason Li, Junkai Zhang

item.title: Approximating Minimum Spanning Trees in Metrics under Semi-Random Corruptions
item.description: arXiv:2610.40594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of finding minimum spanning trees in semi-random corrupted metrics. In this problem proposed by Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), we start with a metric space $\mathcal{M} = (X, d)$. The adversary independently corrupts each pairwise distance with probability $p$. The algorithm only observes these possibly corrupted distances and must output a spanning tree whose expected cost (in the true metric) is multiplicatively close to the minimum spanning tree cost. Prior work showed that losing a factor of $\Omega(\log n)$ is necessary, even if the algorithm may adaptively select $O(n/\log n)$ points and probe the true distances between them. However, no upper bounds were known. We study three regimes based on whether the adversary can only increase, decrease, or arbitrarily change the corrupted distances. We show the following: (1) In the increase-only setting, we give a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. (2) In the decrease-only setting, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. Additionally, we show an $O(\log^4 n)$-approximation algorithm that runs in quasi-polynomial time $n^{O(\log n)}$, for any constant $p \leq 0.1$. Moreover, we show that a polynomial-time algorithm computing an $n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$-approximation is unlikely to exist. (3) In the general setting, where the adversary can both increase and decrease distances, we show an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for every $0 \leq p < \frac{1}{4}$. Further, we show that no $o(n)$-approximation is possible for $\frac{1}{2} \leq p < 1$. Our algorithms answer the main open question in Bateni et al.'s work; moreover, the $O(\log n)$-approximations in the latter two settings are information-theoretically optimal.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Anand, Anupam Gupta, Rajesh Jayaram, Euiwoong Lee, Ali Vakilian

item.title: On Zeros and Algorithms for Disordered Systems II: The Antiferromagnetic Ising Model up to Kesten-Stigum
item.description: arXiv:2610.40598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give the first polynomial-time algorithm to estimate the partition function of the antiferromagnetic Ising model on the uniformly random $d$-regular graph to arbitrarily high accuracy for all inverse temperatures up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold. This is the entire regime in which the model is "replica symmetric," and is conjectured to be optimal for polynomial-time counting and sampling. To achieve our algorithmic result, we establish the absence of Fisher zeros for the partition function in a constant-width strip around the interval from $0$ up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold, with high probability over the randomness of the input graph. AI Disclosure: The overarching vision and proof architecture were developed solely by the authors without AI input. GPT 5.5 Pro was used, with extensive guidance from the authors, for only a few minor technical aspects of the proof. The authors independently verified correctness and wrote everything by hand. We take full responsibility for its contents. A more detailed statement can be found in Section 1.2.
item.dc:creator: Ferenc Bencs, Brice Huang, Daniel Z. Lee, Kuikui Liu, Guus Regts

item.title: Local-to-Global Theorems Based on Cones with Applications to Graph Coloring
item.description: arXiv:2610.37721v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local-to-Global theorems are a cornerstone of many of recent developments in theoretical computer science from coding theory and PCPs all the way to analyzing mixing time of Markov chains. Building on trickledown theorems on simplicial complexes, several techniques have been established to obtain tighter local-to-global theorems to analyze the spectral gap of the Glauber dynamics, namely matrix trickledown, ${\mathcal C}$-Lorentzian polynomials and more recently Bochner type inequalities. In this paper, we adopt non-local local-to-global/Bochner type inequalities on "cones", corresponding to the local neighborhood of a given vertex, to show that the Glauber dynamics mixes in polynomial time to sample proper colorings of maximum degree $\Delta$ graphs as long as $q\geq 1.7408\Delta$.
item.dc:creator: Anqi Li, Shayan Oveis Gharan

item.title: Separations between $\#\mathrm{BIS}$ and $\#\mathrm{IS}$
item.description: arXiv:2610.38164v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give complexity-theoretic separations between $\#\mathrm{BIS}$ and $\#\mathrm{IS}$. Given a graph $G$, and a fugacity $\lambda>0$, the hard-core model is given by $Z_G(\lambda)=\sum_{I\in\mathcal I(G)}\lambda^{|I|}$, where $\mathcal I(G)$ denotes the independent sets of $G$. For $F\ge1$, an $F$-factor approximation to $Z_G(\lambda)$ is an estimate $\widehat Z$ satisfying $F^{-1}Z_G(\lambda)\le\widehat Z\le FZ_G(\lambda)$. Let $\mathcal G_\Delta$ denote the class of $\Delta$-regular graphs and $\mathcal G_{\Delta,\Delta}$ the class of $\Delta$-regular bipartite graphs. We give two separation results. (1) There exist an integer $\Delta\ge3$, a sufficiently large fugacity $\lambda$, and a constant $c>0$ so that the following hold: (a) For every $\delta\in(0,1)$, deterministic $(1+\delta)$-factor approximation on $\mathcal G_{\Delta,\Delta}$ is possible in time $\exp(cn)\operatorname{poly}(n,1/\delta)$. (b) Under the Gap-Exponential Time Hypothesis, there exists no deterministic algorithm running in time $\exp(2cn)\operatorname{poly}(n)$ on $\mathcal G_\Delta$ that gives an $\frac{11}{10}$-factor approximation. (2) For every fixed $\Delta\ge3$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, for all sufficiently large fugacities $\lambda$, the following hold: (a) There exists an algorithm which outputs a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon)^n$-factor approximation to $Z_G(\lambda)$ on $\mathcal G_{\Delta,\Delta}$ in polynomial time. (b) Under the assumption $\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}$, there exists no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm on $\mathcal G_\Delta$ that gives a $(1+\varepsilon)^n$-factor approximation. Both our algorithmic results follow from a new spanning-tree encoding of independent sets that enables an efficient representation of large independent sets.
item.dc:creator: Ijay Narang

item.title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part II: Langevin Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.38206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem on the sphere, in which we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\mathcal{S}_N=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\lVert x\rVert^2=N\}$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. Continuing the program initiated in Part I [arXiv:2610.16705], we show that spherical Langevin dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, our results demonstrate that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.
item.dc:creator: Aniket Das, Tselil Schramm

item.title: Order Maintenance in Worst-Case Constant Time, Verified
item.description: arXiv:2610.38616v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Order maintenance asks for a data structure that keeps a sequence of elements under insertions and deletions and tells which of two elements comes first. We give an algorithm, assembled from published components, that performs each operation in worst-case constant time, and verify it in Lean 4. The algorithm is a program for a random-access machine deeply embedded in Lean, whose interpreter counts every instruction. We prove that the program answers every query as a simple reference specification does, that each operation takes at most a fixed number of steps, independent of the number of elements and of the history, and that after $t$ operations no value it has computed has more than $O(\log t)$ bits, so it runs unchanged on a machine with words of that size. A verified translation that preserves step counts exactly connects the high-level proofs to the machine program, so the interpreter is the only cost model to trust. An unverified native implementation shows the algorithm's practical cost.
item.dc:creator: Denis Firsov

item.title: ExplainCC: Explaining Correlated Clusters by Node Labels
item.description: arXiv:2610.38667v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An increasingly important requirement for clustering algorithms is that decisions and outcomes need to be clearly understandable for human users. We address this requirement for the Correlation Clustering (CC) problem, in case the objects to be clustered are accompanied by labels. In CC one seeks to partition a set of objects into clusters based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity information. Our proposed model only considers clusters that can be explained by a label tree, which is essentially a decision tree that partitions the objects according to labels. The goal is to find an explainable partition of the data that minimizes the CC objective function. We formalize this problem from a theoretical viewpoint, and prove several hardness of approximation results, also when constraining the size of the tree. Our proposed greedy method finds locally optimal splits, and works recursively in a top-down approach. To efficiently compute the best split, we carefully maintain certain counters. An experimental evaluation demonstrates its effectiveness. The proposed algorithm processes graphs with over million edges in a few minutes, can find the ground truth in synthetic data, and is able to produce interpretable clusters in real world networks.
item.dc:creator: Nadeesha Shyami Kumari Herath Mudiyanselage, Florian Adriaens, Nikolaj Tatti

item.title: Complexity of Differentially Private Selection via Federated APIs
item.description: arXiv:2610.38789v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Differential privacy (DP) has become the standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, yet its practical implementation in federated or distributed settings often faces a significant utility gap compared to the central model. While existing frameworks, including local, shuffle, and secure aggregation models, offer vetted primitives, they can incur high error for important tasks such as selection. Our first contribution is to show that this is inherent in the aggregation model: any private selection algorithm relying on the standard noisy aggregation primitive requires $\Omega(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)$ samples. To address this limitation, we propose adding a new primitive that implements a version of the Sparse Vector Technique (SVT) and argue that it has simple implementations under various trust models. We demonstrate its power by developing an $\varepsilon$-differentially private algorithm for the selection problem. For selection in dimension $d$, our algorithm achieves an additive error of $O\left(\frac{\log(dn)}{\varepsilon}\right)$, matching that of the central model when $n$ is polynomially bounded in $d$. Furthermore, we show that this can be done using a near-optimal expected number $O(d\log^*d)$ of SVT queries. Together with existing lower bounds for the shuffle model, this result establishes an exponential separation between the SVT model and shuffle or aggregation-based models. We demonstrate the model's broad applicability to diverse tasks such as $F_p$ loss minimization, heavy-hitter identification, and sparse mean estimation.
item.dc:creator: Hilal Asi, Vitaly Feldman, Jelani Nelson, Huy L. Nguyen, Kunal Talwar, Samson Zhou

item.title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
item.description: arXiv:2610.38955v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize. We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options. Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2\pi X)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.
item.dc:creator: Sudipto Guha

item.title: An Exact Parallel Dense Gauss-Seidel Algorithm with Trade-Offs between Parallel Execution Time and Preprocessing Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.39990v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Gauss-Seidel iterative method is commonly used for solving systems of linear equations because of its good convergence properties. However, the Gauss-Seidel algorithm cannot be easily parallelized because of the data dependencies existing at each iteration. The best parallel execution time for dense systems of equations is $O(n)$ given that enough processors are available and no preprocessing is performed. In this paper we propose a new parallel Gauss-Seidel algorithm which is capable of achieving better parallel runtimes at the expense of more preprocessing time. The algorithm can be tuned in order to provide convenient trade-offs between the preprocessing time and the best parallel runtime achievable by the algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Mugurel-Ionu\c{t} Andreica, Pantelimon George Popescu, Eliana-Dina T\^ir\c{s}a

item.title: Counting approximate breakpoint medians of random genomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.40027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unsigned linear unichromosomal genomes with genes labeled 1, . . . , n are represented by permutations of these labels, whose adjacencies are the unordered pairs of genes occurring consecutively. The breakpoint distance counts the adjacencies of one genome that are absent from the other, and a breakpoint median minimizes the total breakpoint distance to a given set of genomes. Deciding whether a permutation is a median often requires a minimization over the whole symmetric group, which makes the median set resistant to exact counting. We replace this global condition by a local one: a c-approximate median is a genome having at most c adjacencies absent from all the input genomes. For a fixed genome we introduce its approximate median inverse, the set of ordered k-tuples of genomes ad- mitting it as a c-approximate median, and we construct and count this set explicitly. For k genomes chosen uniformly and independently at random, this gives the probability that a given genome is a c-approximate median and the expected number of such approximate medians. The relaxation is not only technical: approximate medians and near-optimal genomes co- incide up to a shift of the tolerance that remains bounded in probability as the number of genes grows. Finally, we derive an explicit upper bound on the probability that a given genome is an exact median, and on the expected number of exact breakpoint medians.
item.dc:creator: Poly H. da Silva, Arash Jamshidpey, David Sankoff

item.title: The Value of Experiments in Assortment Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.40557v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retailers can learn customer preferences by experimenting with different assortments. However, the cost of each experiment and the operational burden of repeatedly changing product offerings can make extensive experimentation impractical. We study how much a retailer can improve its final assortment decision using customer observations from one (or a very small number of) fixed experimental assortments. We consider the multinomial logit model, where product revenues are known but customer preferences are unknown. In this setting, we jointly design the experimental assortment and the rule for selecting a final assortment from observed customer choices to minimize worst-case regret: the expected revenue loss of the final assortment relative to an optimal assortment under the true preferences, maximized over possible customer preferences. We first characterize exactly the minimax regret and an optimal assortment when no experimentation is possible. We then show, surprisingly, that offering a single experimental assortment to just one customer can already substantially reduce regret, depending on how the products' revenues compare. We derive the exact minimax regret and an optimal experimental policy in this setting. When a single fixed experimental assortment is offered to many customers, we give a geometric characterization of the limiting minimax regret and construct an asymptotically optimal policy. Depending on product revenues, this single experiment can yield no improvement over no experimentation or nearly complete regret reduction. Finally, we extend our analysis to multiple experimental assortments chosen in advance, characterizing the limiting minimax regret, constructing asymptotically optimal policies, and identifying which collections of assortments allow worst-case regret to vanish as the number of customer observations grows.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadreza Ahmadnejadsaein, Amine Bennouna, Omar El Housni

item.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.40562v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-\textsf{Majority}, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-\textsf{Majority} achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-\textsf{Majority} that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.
item.dc:creator: Francesco d'Amore, Joel Rybicki, Nobutaka Shimizu, Takeharu Shiraga, Robin Vacus

item.title: When Imputation Changes the Nearest Neighbor: Exact Certification of Similarity Retrieval for Incomplete Sensor Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.40579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sensor time series routinely reach similarity search with missing values, and the retrieved neighbours then depend on how the gaps were filled. We ask which retrieval conclusions hold for every admissible completion of an incomplete query. For a family of window-minimum distances that contains the $L_1$ distance as its separable end we give a pairwise certificate that one candidate is strictly closer than another, a guaranteed candidate set that contains every possible nearest neighbour, and a certificate that a nearest-neighbour label cannot change. The guarantees hold uniformly over the specified box and apply to the true query whenever it lies inside. At the separable end a closed form is known, but beyond it the worst-case gap need not be attained at a corner of the box. We prove a finite reduction to critical values, give an exact interval dynamic programme for the worst-case ranking gap, and a quadratic-time fast layer of valid bounds and feasible witnesses, supported by an exact criterion for when the feature-box relaxation is tight. On three traffic-sensor collections with real gap patterns, linear interpolation changes the nearest neighbour in 15 to 33 percent of the queries. At the full band the feature-box relaxation misses up to 14 percent of the exactly stable boundary pairs, whereas fixed-completion and Monte Carlo checks issue false certificates. The fast layer resolves about 90 percent of all tested boundary pairs without dynamic programming, and on paired network-scale queries the exact method is 82 to 110 times faster than the programme alone. Label certificates transfer to three public benchmarks, and the band width trades forecasting accuracy and certification coverage for lower imputation sensitivity, with dataset-dependent crossovers.
item.dc:creator: Jianru Shen

item.title: Uniform Capacitated Clustering with Few Extra Centers
item.description: arXiv:2610.40625v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In uniform capacitated $(k,z)$-clustering, we open $k$ centers and assign every client to a center so that no center serves more than $U$ clients, minimizing the sum of the $z$-th powers of the assignment distances; $k$-median and $k$-means are the cases $z=1$ and $z=2$. We study algorithms that may open $k+\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ centers for a fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ and must respect the capacities exactly. In low dimensions, we give deterministic algorithms that are, except for $k$-median in the plane, the first polynomial-time algorithms with $(1+\varepsilon)k$ centers whose ratio is bounded independently of $\varepsilon$. In Euclidean space of any dimension, with clients of bounded doubling dimension, the ratio is $\mathcal{B}_z-(\mathcal{B}_z-1)\varepsilon+\delta$ for every fixed $\delta>0$, where $\mathcal{B}_z<3^z$ for $z>1$; this is $3-2\varepsilon+\delta$ for $k$-median and $5-4\varepsilon+\delta$ for $k$-means. In doubling metrics, the ratio is $3^z-(3^z-1)\varepsilon+\delta$ when centers may share a location, and a constant otherwise, such as $\min\{7-4\varepsilon,\,3+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)\}+\delta$ for $k$-median. In general metrics, deleting centers greedily gives ratio $3+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)+\delta$ for $k$-median when centers may share a location and $7+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)+\delta$ otherwise, improving the previous $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$. Our main tool is a rescue lemma. Splitting a near-optimal uncapacitated solution gives at most $2k-1$ blocks of at most $U$ clients, and giving a block a private center saves its share of the extra cost of following an optimal solution. Since a center of the optimal solution can be closed once all its blocks are rescued, $\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ extra centers save almost an $\varepsilon$-fraction of this extra cost instead of an $\varepsilon/2$-fraction.
item.dc:creator: Kangke Cheng, Guanlin Mo, Hu Ding

item.title: Sublinear Algorithms for Estimating Single-Linkage Clustering Costs
item.description: arXiv:2510.11547v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Single-linkage clustering (SLC) is a fundamental method for hierarchical data analysis. In the distance setting, a $k$-clustering produced by SLC can be obtained by computing a minimum spanning tree (MST) and deleting its $k-1$ heaviest edges. This naturally induces a cost profile for the SLC hierarchy: for each $k\in[n]$, we define $\mathrm{cost}_k$ to be the weight of the resulting $k$-component spanning forest, equivalently, the minimum total weight of any spanning forest with exactly $k$ connected components. The corresponding \emph{SLC cost profile} is $(\mathrm{cost}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{cost}_n)$, and the scalar quantity $\mathrm{cost}(G)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathrm{cost}_k$ is the area under this profile. We study the problem of approximating these quantities in sublinear time. We assume that the input is a weighted graph $G$ of average degree $d$ with edge weights in $\{1,\dots,W\}$, accessed through adjacency-list queries; missing edges are treated as having infinite distance. Our main result is a sampling-based algorithm that outputs a succinct sketch of the entire SLC cost profile in the distance setting. The algorithm runs in $\widetilde{O}(d\sqrt{W}/\varepsilon^3)$ time and returns a sketch from which one can derive estimates $(\widehat{\mathrm{cost}}_1,\ldots,\widehat{\mathrm{cost}}_n)$ satisfying $\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl|\widehat{\mathrm{cost}}_k-\mathrm{cost}_k\bigr| \le \varepsilon\,\mathrm{cost}(G)$. Thus, we obtain an $\ell_1$ approximation to the full profile whose error is at most an $\varepsilon$-fraction of the area under the true profile. In particular, this yields a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-approximation to $\mathrm{cost}(G)$ within the same running time. We also prove a nearly matching lower bound of $\Omega(d\sqrt{W}/\varepsilon^2)$ queries for estimating $\mathrm{cost}(G)$.
item.dc:creator: Pan Peng, Christian Sohler, Yi Xu

item.title: A Logic-based Algorithmic Meta-Theorem for Treedepth: Single Exponential FPT Time and Polynomial Space
item.description: arXiv:2510.19793v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a graph $G$, the parameter treedepth measures the minimum depth among all forests $F$, called elimination forests, such that $G$ is a subgraph of the ancestor-descendant closure of $F$. We introduce a logic, called neighborhood operator logic with acyclicity, connectivity and clique constraints ($\mathsf{NEO}_2[\mathsf{FRec}]+\mathsf{ACK}$ for short), that captures all NP-hard problems like Independent Set or Hamiltonian Cycle that are known to be tractable in time $2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ and space $n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ on $n$-vertex graphs provided with elimination forests of depth $k$. We provide a model checking algorithm for $\mathsf{NEO}_2[\mathsf{FRec}]+\mathsf{ACK}$ with such complexity that unifies and extends these results. For $\mathsf{NEO}_2[\mathsf{FRec}]+\mathsf{k}$, the fragment of the above logic that does not use acyclicity and connectivity constraints, we get a strengthening of this result, where the space complexity is reduced to $\mathcal{O}(k\log(n))$. With a similar mechanism as the distance neighborhood logic introduced in [Bergougnoux, Dreier and Jaffke, SODA 2023], the logic $\mathsf{NEO}_2[\mathsf{FRec}]+\mathsf{ACK}$ is an extension of the fully-existential $\mathsf{MSO}_2$ with predicates for (1) querying generalizations of the neighborhoods of vertex sets, (2) verifying the connectivity and acyclicity of vertex and edge sets, and (3) verifying that a vertex set induces a clique. Our results provide $2^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ time and $n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ space algorithms for problems for which the existence of such algorithms was previously unknown. In particular, $\mathsf{NEO}_2[\mathsf{FRec}]$ captures CNF-SAT via the incidence graphs associated to CNF formulas, and it also captures several modulo counting problems like Odd Dominating Set.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Bergougnoux, Vera Chekan, Giannos Stamoulis

item.title: Sampling Sphere Packings with Continuum Glauber Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2601.18748v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuum Glauber dynamics is a spatial birth-death process whose stationary distribution is a Gibbs distribution. We establish a spectral gap for Continuum Glauber dynamics applied to Gibbs point processes with repulsive pair potentials, a well-known special case of which is the hard sphere model. For arbitrary-range repulsive pair potentials, we show that a continuous version of Spectral Independence suffices to establish a spectral gap. This extends the regime of activity for which Continuum Glauber dynamics is known to mix, yielding a simple efficient sampling algorithm for arbitrary-range pair potentials that matches the known efficient sampling regime for finite-range pair potentials currently based on specialized algorithms. As a consequence, we also improve the threshold up to which packings of fixed size/density can be efficiently sampled from a bounded domain, the first improvement since Kannan, Mahoney and Montenegro (2003). To prove these results, we develop continuous analogs of Spectral Independence and negative fields localization. We show that a stronger variant of zero-freeness implies Spectral Independence, which in turn allows us to run the localization scheme to boost the spectral gap of Continuum Glauber dynamics from smaller activity to larger activity. While this follows the high-level blueprint of Chen and Eldan (2022) for the discrete setting, we have to address several novel difficulties due to the continuous setting. Notably, we avoid discretization in the algorithm and the analysis and work directly in the continuous setting.
item.dc:creator: Aiya Kuchukova, Santosh S. Vempala, Daniel J. Zhang

item.title: Model checking with temporal graphs and their derivative
item.description: arXiv:2602.12446v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temporal graphs are graphs where the presence or properties of their vertices and edges change over time. When time is discrete, a temporal graph can be defined as a sequence of static graphs over a discrete time span, called lifetime, or as a single graph where each edge is associated with a specific set of time instants where the edge is alive. For static graphs, Courcelle's Theorem asserts that any graph problem expressible in monadic second-order logic can be solved in linear time on graphs of bounded tree-width. We propose the first adaptation of Courcelle's Theorem for monadic second-order logic on temporal graphs that does not explicitly rely on a parameter proportional to the lifetime, or defined as the maximum number of time-edges incident with any vertex which in the worst case is higher than the lifetime. We then introduce the notion of derivative over a sliding time window of a chosen size, and define the tree-width and twin-width of the temporal graph's derivative. We exemplify its usefulness with meta-theorems with respect to a temporal variant of first-order logic. The resulting logic expresses a wide range of temporal graph problems including a version of temporal cliques, an important notion when querying time series databases for community structures.
