item.dc:creator: Binh-Minh Bui-Xuan, Florent Krasnopol, Bruno Monasson, Nathalie Sznajder

item.title: Parameterized Algorithms for Computing MAD Trees
item.description: arXiv:2603.29381v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the well-studied problem of finding a spanning tree with minimum average distance between vertex pairs (called a MAD tree). This is a classic network design problem which is known to be NP-hard. While approximation algorithms and polynomial-time algorithms for some graph classes are known, the parameterized complexity of the problem has not been investigated so far. We start a parameterized complexity analysis with the goal of determining the border of algorithmic tractability for the MAD tree problem. To this end, we provide a linear-time algorithm for graphs of constant modular width and a polynomial-time algorithm for graphs of bounded treewidth; the degree of the polynomial depends on the treewidth. That is, the problem is in FPT with respect to modular width and in XP with respect to treewidth. Moreover, we show that it is in FPT when parameterized by vertex integrity, by maximum leaf number, or by an above-guarantee parameter. We complement these algorithms with NP-hardness on split graphs.
item.dc:creator: Tom-Lukas Breitkopf, Vincent Froese, Anton Herrmann, Andr\'e Nichterlein, Camille Richer

item.title: Deterministic Streaming Lower Bounds for Approximate Maximum Clique and Maximum Independent Set
item.description: arXiv:2609.18635v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the canonical \textsf{Maximum Clique} and \textsf{Maximum Independent Set} problems in the one-pass edge-arrival graph streaming setting. Here, the edges of some input graph $G = (V,E)$ are presented one at a time (possibly including deletions), before an algorithm needs to produce either a large clique or independent set at the end of the stream, with the focus being on space complexity. We are interested in finding $\beta$-approximate solutions, for any $\beta \geq 1$. Previous work gave an algorithm using $\tilde{O}\left(n^2/\beta^2\right)$ bits of space, together with a corresponding $\tilde{\Omega}\left(n^2/\beta^2\right)$ two-party communication lower bound [Halld\'orsson et al., ICALP'12], seeming to resolve the problem. However, their algorithm crucially relies on randomness, and the best known deterministic algorithm remains a folklore derandomisation using $O\left(n^2/\beta\right)$ bits of space, leaving a (deterministic) gap of size $\tilde{O}(\beta)$. We make progress towards this gap with a strong lower bound for a restricted range of $\beta$: whenever $\beta \leq \sqrt{n}/36\log n$, any deterministic algorithm for either problem must use $\Omega\left(\frac{n^2}{\beta\cdot\log n}\right)$ bits of space. Our proof is via a two-party one-way communication lower bound, and highlights the power of randomness when approaching either of these problems.
item.dc:creator: Adithya Diddapur

item.title: Online Stochastic Allocation with Increasing Returns
item.description: arXiv:2609.34121v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online allocation with increasing returns, where an uncertain number of customers arrive sequentially and can be irrevocably assigned to any product with remaining capacity. Each assignment earns a base reward plus a bonus that is nondecreasing in the number of previous assignments to the same product. Prior work has focused primarily on fixed or diminishing returns. Under increasing returns, the central challenge is that concentrating assignments can unlock large future rewards, while a different product may be preferable if arrivals stop early. We show that classical approaches, including greedy and natural LP-based rounding algorithms, can perform arbitrarily poorly, even with homogeneous bonuses. We evaluate performance through competitive ratios relative to the hindsight offline optimum. For homogeneous bonuses, we establish a tight competitive ratio of $1/2$. For arbitrary heterogeneous bonuses, however, no online algorithm can guarantee a competitive ratio greater than $1/m$, where $m$ is the number of products. By imposing discrete concavity on the bonus functions, we limit the concentration of rewards in later assignments and restore constant guarantees. Under this structure, we develop a re-solving framework that repeatedly selects a planning horizon, constructs a feasible allocation plan from the current state, and executes its assignments in a specific order. For arbitrary arrival distributions, we design distribution-oblivious deterministic and randomized algorithms with competitive ratios of $0.2537$ and $0.3864$, respectively. For known increasing-failure-rate (IFR) arrival distributions, we exploit distributional information to obtain a deterministic $1/2$-competitive algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Shuo Sun, Yunduan Lin

item.title: A Deterministic Near-Linear Time Approximation Algorithm for Restricted Shortest Paths in Directed Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.18337v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the restricted shortest paths problem, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge directed graph $G$ whose edges are assigned two non-negative weights (or resources) called lengths and costs, a source vertex $s$, and a cost threshold $C$. The goal is to find, for each target vertex $t$, the length of the shortest $(s,t)$-path whose total cost is at most $C$. Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, and Karczmarz (SODA 2025) gave the first randomized bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm on directed graphs running in sub-$mn$ time, answering a problem posed by Bernstein (SODA 2012). We substantially improve this on two fronts, supplying a deterministic bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time. Our approach straightforwardly generalizes to more than two resources. For $k$ resources, a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon_1,\ldots,1+\varepsilon_k)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time is possible, with $\varepsilon_1=\ldots=\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: Vikrant Ashvinkumar

item.title: Multidimensional Online Resource Allocation for Large Language Model Services under Nonstationary Demand
item.description: arXiv:2302.08234v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study multidimensional online generalized assignment under nonstationary arrivals, motivated by resource allocation for large language model agent services. Providers may commit model and tool allowances to agent tasks upon admission, reserving budgets for their internal execution loops. Each request is rejected or accepted with an irrevocable assignment to one compatible server, earning reward and consuming a vector of its nonreplenishing budgets. Arrivals are independent with known, potentially time-varying type distributions. Scalar reductions can discard feasible combinations of requests with complementary resource requirements. To maximize expected reward, we develop Vector-Aware Best-Fit, which combines linear-programming-guided candidate routing with calibrated acceptance while retaining vector feasibility. Relative to the expected clairvoyant offline optimum, its guarantee improves on scalar reduction in the multidimensional case and has the best possible inverse-dimensional order. With an appropriate acceptance parameter, the proposed policy attains the optimal competitive ratio on all-heavy instances, where every feasible assignment consumes more than half of at least one resource budget. We further develop two heuristics that retain its performance guarantee. Computational results show that the heuristics perform well against benchmarks in most tested settings, especially when capacity is scarce relative to demand.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wang, Zihao Li, Zhenzhen Yan

item.title: A Competitive Algorithm for Agnostic Active Learning
item.description: arXiv:2310.18786v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For some hypothesis classes and input distributions, active agnostic learning needs exponentially fewer samples than passive learning; for other classes and distributions, it offers little to no improvement. The most popular algorithms for agnostic active learning express their performance in terms of a parameter called the disagreement coefficient, but it is known that these algorithms are inefficient on some inputs. We take a different approach to agnostic active learning, getting an algorithm that is competitive with the optimal algorithm for any binary hypothesis class $H$ and distribution $D_X$ over $X$. In particular, if any algorithm can use $m^*$ queries to get $O(\eta)$ error, then our algorithm uses $O(m^* \log |H|)$ queries to get $O(\eta)$ error. Our algorithm lies in the vein of the splitting-based approach of Dasgupta [2004], which gets a similar result for the realizable ($\eta = 0$) setting. We also show that it is NP-hard to do better than our algorithm's $O(\log |H|)$ overhead in general.
item.dc:creator: Eric Price, Yihan Zhou

item.title: A quantum central path algorithm for linear optimization
item.description: arXiv:2311.03977v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a novel quantum algorithm for solving linear optimization problems by quantum-mechanical simulation of the central path. While interior point methods follow the central path with an iterative algorithm that works with successive linearizations of the perturbed KKT conditions, we perform a simulation working directly with the nonlinear complementarity equations. Using a two-stage quantum eigenpath traversal schedule, this approach yields an algorithm for solving linear optimization problems involving $m$ constraints and $n$ variables to $\varepsilon$-optimality using $\widetilde{O}\!\left((m+n)^{3/2}\,\varepsilon^{-1}+(m+n)^{1/2}\,\varepsilon^{-3/2}\right)$ queries to an oracle that evaluates a potential function. In the standard gate model (i.e., without access to quantum RAM), our algorithm can obtain $\varepsilon$-precise solutions to LO problems using at most $$\widetilde{O}\!\left(\left[\frac{(m+n)^{3/2}}{\varepsilon} + \frac{(m+n)^{1/2}}{\varepsilon^{3/2}}\right] \cdot \mathrm{nnz}(A)\right)$$ elementary gates, where $\mathrm{nnz}(A)$ is the total number of non-zero elements found in the constraint matrix.
item.dc:creator: Brandon Augustino, Jiaqi Leng, Jialu Bao, Giacomo Nannicini, Tam\'as Terlaky, Xiaodi Wu

item.title: Adaptive Allele-Haplotype Incidence Indexing for Pangenome Queries: Representation, Reconstruction, and Benchmarking
item.description: arXiv:2512.21320v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Population-scale analysis of phased genetic variants requires both allele-carrier retrieval and ordered haplotype context. We examine H1, an adaptive allele-haplotype incidence-row index, and H2, a canonical edge-path representation derived from a fixed, nonoverlapping variant catalog. We prove conditional reconstruction of abstract H2 walks and distinguish this property from unrestricted equivalence to genomic variation graphs. A completed local notebook experiment used a chromosome 1 interval (20-22 Mb), 200 diploid individuals, 24,921 SNV/indel records, and 45 SVTYPE-annotated records. For 24,966 extracted nonreference rows across 400 haplotypes, the serialized H1 incidence-row files occupied 0.872 MiB with a simple adaptive layout and 1.126 MiB with a custom Roaring-like layout, versus 1.190 MiB for a bitmap-payload baseline; a whole-file Zstandard archive of the adaptive layout occupied 0.207 MiB. For a separately constructed nonoverlapping SNV projection containing 22,727 sites, indexed H2 edge sequences occupied 75,130,882 bytes in a raw format and 5,156,418 bytes with context-Huffman encoding (14.57-fold reduction). Carrier-equivalence and graph-adjacency assertions passed in the notebook, but full crosscallset phasing, nucleotide-level SV reconstruction, and comparison with production indexes remain unresolved. The measurements establish a restricted implementation feasibility result, not superior end-to-end pangenome compression.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Garrone

item.title: Density Decomposition on Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.07794v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hypergraphs capture higher-order interactions involving multiple entities. Existing decomposition models, such as $k$-core and nbr-$k$-core, rely on degree or neighborhood constraints and may overlook fine-grained density variations. We propose a $(k,\delta)$-dense subhypergraph model based on capped hyperedge contributions. For each parameter pair, the unique dense set is the inclusionwise smallest maximizer of a penalized capped hyperedge contribution. These dense sets form a nested hierarchy characterized by egalitarian $\delta$-orientations and hypergraph reachability. We develop three algorithms for dense subhypergraph search and two for complete density decomposition. Both decomposition algorithms use integral flow balancing: Flow-Decomp extracts density levels through strongly connected component condensation, while Reverse-Decomp uses direct reverse propagation. Once an egalitarian orientation is obtained, both recover all density levels in linear time. We further derive sandwich bounds that restrict computation to equivalent residual subproblems and develop incremental algorithms for maintaining the hierarchy under hyperedge insertions and deletions. Experiments on nine real-world hypergraphs, including datasets with over 15 million vertices, compare our methods with four established decomposition models. The results show that Reverse-Decomp improves decomposition efficiency, incremental maintenance outperforms recomputation in the tested settings, and the proposed model captures density structures overlooked by degree-based decompositions.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Leng, Hongchao Qin, Rong-Hua Li, Guoren Wang

item.title: Express Language Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2606.10944v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a new tool, Express, for converting a non-causal attention approximation into a causal approximation with matching approximation guarantees. When combined with the state-of-the-art Thinformer approximation, Express improves upon the best known causal attention guarantees, delivering $\log^{3/2}(n)/s$ approximation error with only $O(s)$ memory and $O(s^2 \log^2(n))$ compression overhead for a sequence of length $n$. We pair these developments with an efficient I/O-aware Triton implementation, demonstrate substantial speedups over FlashAttention 2, and use Express to overcome four resource bottlenecks in the language modeling pipeline: long-context prefill, KV cache compression, long-form memory-constrained decoding, and long-form compute-constrained decoding.
item.dc:creator: Albert Gong, Annabelle Michael Carrell, Raaz Dwivedi, Lester Mackey

item.title: Self-Referential $K$-SAT and the Finite Analogue of G\"odel's Incompleteness Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2607.01671v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study self-reference and solution independence in Boolean $K$-SAT as a finite analogue of G\"{o}del incompleteness. Independence is defined through factorial moments of the solution count. Constant-width random formulas fail this criterion due to correlations among overlapping assignments. At a covering threshold, logarithmic-width random CNFs have a Poisson solution count, with positive probabilities of unsatisfiability and unique satisfiability. Replacing a redundant clause by one falsified by the unique solution yields an unsatisfiable companion preserving the unsigned incidence graph. For every permitted local view of a good uniquely satisfiable formula, an unsatisfiable companion preserves that view. Irreducibility defeats deterministic and bounded-error evaluators using $N^c$ clause queries, for fixed $0<c<1$. It establishes a local information obstruction, not an unrestricted time lower bound. For fixed $\delta>0$, transcripts of $N^{1-\delta}$ queries leave $N-o(N)$ bits of witness entropy. On typical support graphs, expansion yields linear Resolution width, linear PC/PCR and SOS degree, and exponential proof size. Bounds hold for semantic Cutting Planes under a partition condition and for Positivstellensatz with bounded product width, uniformly over unsatisfiable support-preserving signings. Structural evidence and the limits of acceleration strategies motivate the self-referential $K$-SAT exhaustive-search hypothesis (SRK-ESH): no uniform deterministic algorithm deciding the promise family achieves a fixed proportional saving in the exponent. This dual-evidence criterion combines intrinsic hardness mechanisms with algorithmic evidence. We interpret this hypothesis as a quantitative projection of the G\"{o}del-style local--global gap. The information obstruction constrains quantum local observation and statistical learning from bounded local information.
item.dc:creator: Wen Fang, Xianxian Li, Jun Liu, Jie Luo, Yongxin Tong, Ke Xu

item.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2607.15530v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent'' step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a normalized variant instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iterate normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $\epsilon$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $\tau$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.
item.dc:creator: Arya Mazumdar, Prateeti Mukherjee

item.title: The Polynomial-Time Low-Degree Conjecture is False
item.description: arXiv:2607.20318v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The low-degree method and its associated lower bounds are widely used to guide algorithm design and to provide evidence of computational hardness in average-case inference, high-dimensional statistics, random optimization, and related problems. This led to the low-degree conjecture, which predicts that when the low-degree advantage between a planted distribution and a uniform null distribution remains bounded, no efficient distinguisher can succeed after independent noise, provided that the planted distribution has permutation symmetry. Several works have produced counterexamples to variants of this conjecture or to versions for algorithms with higher time complexity, but the conjecture remained open in its standard binary, polynomial-time formulation. We disprove the polynomial-time low-degree conjecture by giving a family of examples. For every fixed integer $r\geq3$, we construct a permutation-invariant distribution $\mathbb{P}_n$ on simple graphs, with $\mathbb{Q}_n=G(n,1/2)$, such that every marginal of $\mathbb{P}_n$ on at most $D_n=\Theta((\log n)^{r-1})$ edges is uniform. Therefore, the low-degree advantage is zero through degree $D_n$. Nevertheless, after every edge is independently resampled at a fixed positive rate, a deterministic rank test strongly distinguishes the resulting distribution from $\mathbb{Q}_n$ in linear time in the graph input size. The construction chooses a subspace of a Reed--Muller code whose nonzero polynomials have small absolute bias, selects points whose evaluation vectors have no short linear dependencies, and evaluates a random alternating bilinear form on pairs of these vectors. Our result shows that low-degree indistinguishability, a uniform null distribution, permutation invariance, and independent resampling do not by themselves imply polynomial-time hardness, and suggests that a valid general conjecture must impose an additional condition.

item.title: Group Isomorphism and the Polylogarithmic-Time Hierarchy: Depth-2$\frac{1}{2}$ Circuits and Lower Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2608.26257v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the low-depth circuit complexity of Group Isomorphism in the multiplication (Cayley) table model. We prove the first circuit lower bounds for Group Isomorphism: namely, we show that every family of depth-$2$ Boolean circuits deciding Group Isomorphism requires quasipolynomial-size. (We also extend this to a limited class of depth-3 circuits, namely $\textsf{CNF}$-of-$\textsf{XOR}$s.) We complement this with upper bounds of uniform depth-$2\frac{1}{2}$ circuits of quasipolynomial-size: depth 3 circuits with poly-logarithmic bottom fan-in. A sequence of previous results from 1970-2025 progressively reduced the circuit depth from polynomial to $3\frac{1}{2}$; all of these results relied on the generator-enumerator strategy and, in fact, applied more generally to quasigroups. In contrast, our depth-$2\frac{1}{2}$ construction follows a fundamentally different strategy that exploits structure more specific to groups. We guess a composition series for each group, together with generators for its terms and the isomorphism types of its composition factors. We then inductively verify that the corresponding extensions at each level of the two composition series are compatible. A central part in this approach brings to bear the extensive work on the Short Presentation Conjecture, in tandem with the algorithmic theory of group extensions and cohomology.

item.title: Quantum lower bounds for convex optimization and real matrix-vector query problems
item.description: arXiv:2609.05679v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We (the author and the AI systems that did the heavy lifting) show that the quantum query complexity of minimizing a convex function over a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with evaluation and membership queries is $\tilde\Omega(n)$, nearly matching the best known upper bound. In particular, we show this even for quadratic minimization, which is equivalent to inverting an $n \times n$ real matrix using matrix-vector queries. We also show linear or nearly linear lower bounds on the quantum query complexity of computing the trace, the sign of the determinant, and the magnitude of the determinant of a real matrix in the matrix-vector query model. We use a novel quantum lower bound technique, the determinantal witness method, based on identifying a witness whose Fourier transform vanishes on low-rank matrices and that correlates well with the function being computed.
